JSON: Name: cnidarian_dna_sleep_pipeline Title: Comparative experimental pipeline to test whether induced neuronal DNA damage drives sleep pressure and whether sleep reduces neuronal DNA damage in two cnidarian species Short Hypothesis: Acute induction of neuronal DNA damage causally increases sleep drive—manifested as increased total sleep time, longer sleep bouts, and elevated arousal threshold—in both Cassiopea and Nematostella. Related Work: Behavioral definition of sleep in non-mammalian organisms relies on immobility, elevated arousal threshold, and homeostatic rebound; prior cnidarian studies established sleep-like states in Hydra and Cassiopea using pulsation or immobility metrics and showed melatonin can modulate quiescence. In bilaterians, multiple reports demonstrate accumulation of neuronal DNA damage during wakefulness and partial repair during sleep, with sleep loss increasing γH2AX and other DNA damage markers. Existing approaches either (1) use EEG-based electrophysiology in mammals, (2) rely on coarse behavioral proxies in invertebrates without cell-type resolution, or (3) demonstrate correlational increases in DNA damage after wakefulness but lack controlled causal perturbations in basal metazoans. Limitations: few cross-species, cross-chronotype comparisons; limited single-cell/neuron-resolved measurements in invertebrates; insufficient causal perturbation (direct chemical/UV induction of DNA damage vs sleep measures) in cnidarians; and incomplete integration of genetic (clock mutants) and pharmacological manipulations to distinguish circadian vs homeostatic drivers. Abstract: This pipeline defines a controlled experimental framework to test the causal effect of neuronal DNA damage on sleep drive and the converse effect of sleep on genome stability in two cnidarian models with divergent chronotypes: diurnal Cassiopea and crepuscular Nematostella. The approach combines automated behavioral monitoring (pulsation rate or pixel-change locomotion), defined arousal-threshold assays, timed perturbations to induce DNA damage (UVB irradiation and the topoisomerase II poison etoposide), pharmacological modulation (melatonin), and neuron-resolved quantification of DNA damage using γH2AX immunofluorescence in transgenic and wild-type animals. The main contribution is a standardized comparative experimental pipeline that (i) quantifies sleep architecture and arousal thresholds across species and genotypes, (ii) measures temporal dynamics of neuronal DNA damage after wakefulness and after sleep or pharmacological intervention, and (iii) tests causality by correlating induced DNA damage with subsequent changes in sleep metrics. Expected outcomes are demonstration of a reproducible, species-independent link between induced neuronal DNA damage and increased sleep drive and a mapped temporal profile of damage accumulation and recovery at single-neuron resolution. Experiments: Species and genotypes: Cassiopea andromeda (wild-type, n ≥ 26 per condition) and Nematostella vectensis (WT and NvClkΔ/Δ mutant; transgenic tg(-2.4NvElav1b:mOrangeCAAX) for neuronal imaging; n ≥ 24 per genotype per condition). Housing and entrainment: 72 h LD (12:12) baseline; additional conditions DD, LL, LDLD as required. Behavioral datasets: continuous video (5 s frame sampling, IR for dark) for 48–72 h per cohort; field pulsation dataset from wild Cassiopea (n ≥ 600 individuals) for validation. Perturbations and groups (all with vehicle controls): (1) Acute UVB: Cassiopea 15 min (312 nm) at ZT8; Nematostella 60 min at ZT8. (2) Etoposide 10 μM exposure at ZT8 for Nematostella. (3) Sleep deprivation (SD): hourly gentle water turbulence for 6–8 h during peak sleep. (4) Melatonin 100 μM or ethanol vehicle administered at active-phase and rest-phase timepoints. (5) Genetic comparison: NvClkΔ/Δ vs WT. Imaging and endpoints: fix at baseline (pre-treatment), 1 h post-treatment, and 48 h post-treatment; dissect peri-rhopalial/rhopalia tissue or ectodermal column, immunostain for γH2AX and DAPI; image with confocal microscopy; quantify γH2AX foci per nucleus in mOrange+ neurons (10–100 cells per sample; ≥ 8 samples per timepoint). Behavioral metrics: percent sleep (fraction quiescent per hour), mean sleep-bout duration, number of sleep bouts, arousal threshold (latency to light/food stimulus), sleep rebound magnitude post-SD, Lomb-Scargle period for rhythmicity, pulsation rate. Molecular metrics: normalized γH2AX foci per nucleus, proportion of neurons with >1 foci, survival/viability at 48h. Baselines: untreated (entrained) and vehicle controls; SD alone; UV/Eto without melatonin; melatonin alone. Statistical plan: mixed-effects models with fixed effects (treatment, species, genotype, timepoint) and random effects (animal, rhopalium), repeated-measures ANOVA or nonparametric equivalents, multiple-test correction (Benjamini-Hochberg), effect-size reporting (Cohen’s d). Comparisons/ablations: (A) UV vs control: test increase in γH2AX at 1 h and increase in sleep within next 24 h. (B) Etoposide vs control: same endpoints. (C) Melatonin vs vehicle during active phase: test reduction in γH2AX and change in sleep metrics. (D) SD vs control: test increase in γH2AX and impaired DNA damage recovery. (E) NvClkΔ/Δ vs WT: test circadian modulation of damage–sleep coupling. (F) Ablation: neuron vs non-neuron foci comparison to test cell-type specificity. Correlation and causal inference: linear mixed models and mediation analysis to quantify whether induced DNA damage predicts subsequent sleep increase and whether sleep duration predicts γH2AX reduction at 48 h. Minimum reported sample sizes, raw images, and analysis code will be provided. Risk Factors and Limitations: Antibody specificity and signal interpretation: γH2AX antibodies validated in vertebrates may have reduced specificity or cross-reactivity in cnidarian tissues, leading to false positives or negatives. Behavioral classification: pulsation- or pixel-change-based sleep metrics risk misclassification due to species-specific low-amplitude motor patterns, size-dependent pulsation rates, or transient environmental disturbances; threshold-optimization may overfit to laboratory conditions and not generalize to field data. Treatment confounds: UV and etoposide produce pleiotropic effects (oxidative stress, membrane damage, altered locomotion) that can change behavior independently of DNA damage; melatonin has antioxidant properties and may reduce DNA damage via non-sleep mechanisms, confounding causal interpretation. Genetic and transgenic constraints: NvClkΔ/Δ and tg(-2.4NvElav1b:mOrangeCAAX) lines may carry background mutations or expression variability that affect sleep or DNA repair pathways. Sampling and throughput: confocal imaging throughput limits per-group sample sizes for neuronal γH2AX quantification; small n reduces power and increases type II error risk. Environmental variability: field validation faces uncontrolled light, temperature, and symbiont-driven ROS variability that limit reproducibility. Generalization: results from two cnidarian species may not extrapolate to other basal metazoans or bilaterians. Computational risks: automated tracking pipelines may fail on low-contrast or occluded frames, introducing measurement bias. Statistical risks: multiple comparisons across species, timepoints, and assays increase false-discovery potential if not rigorously corrected.
